finding: First (from 7 Oct 2022) and last (to 23 Aug 2023) months are partial, so raw monthly alert counts are not comparable.
action: Use full months (Nov 2022 to Jul 2023) or per-day rates for stability checks. Done: all monthly figures use full months.

finding: 417 transactions with a domestic payment type have different sender and receiver countries.
action: Confirm the payment-type mapping. For this review, use bank locations (not payment type) to define cross-border. Done in R3; mapping question still with data owner.

finding: 155,692 domestic UK transactions are paid or received in a foreign currency.
action: Clarify what the currency fields mean before using currency mismatch as a rule input. Not used in R1 to R3.

finding: Structuring is receiver-side and slow: 75 receiving accounts get about 25 payments each from different senders over roughly 180 days, mostly between GBP 2,000 and 9,000.
action: Design R1 on the receiving account with a lookback of at least 90 days; test 30, 90 and 180 days. Tested 91 vs 182 days: 182 days adds detection (option E) but doubles R1 alerts. 30 days not tested, because structuring spreads over about 180 days.

finding: Normal look-alike behaviours are very large (Normal_Fan_Out 2.3m, Normal_Fan_In 2.1m transactions) and will drive false alerts in fan-in, fan-out and pass-through logic.
action: Report false alerts by look-alike behaviour for each rule. Done: Normal_Small_Fan_Out, Normal_Group, Normal_Fan_In and Normal_Fan_Out cause most false alerts in all three rules.

finding: The data has no definition of higher-risk locations, which R3 needs.
action: Obtain the official list. Changed approach: a list derived from this data's laundering labels would be circular, so R3 uses all cross-border payments without a location list until compliance provides one.

finding: R2 has no upper limit on outflow: an account that receives GBP 5,320 and pays out GBP 18,635 in a week is alerted as pass-through, although it is spending its balance.
action: Add an upper bound on outflow relative to inflow, in line with the requirement 'most incoming money leaves again'. Tested on Day 3 (caps of 130% and 110%): rejected, because the cap also removes real pass-through laundering and costs 8 to 11 points of detection.

finding: Detection depends on which accounts count: R1 catches 89% of the 75 structuring collecting accounts but only 4% of the 1,870 one-off senders.
action: Decide whether detection is measured per account or per scheme (collecting account). Report both in the decision proposal.

finding: Alert volumes rise from November to July (R2 +78%, R3 +34%) while transaction volume is flat; R1 is low in the first months because its 91-day lookback has little history.
action: Compare options on the same months only; exclude the R1 warm-up period from stability checks. Done: options compared on full months and on a steady-state period (May to Jul 2023).

finding: The first definition of a true alert (any laundering by the account within the lookback) made a longer R1 lookback look better automatically: only 42% of R1 true alerts under the 182-day option involved laundering money flowing into the account, which is what R1 checks.
action: Changed to: an alert is true only if laundering appears in the activity the rule checks (R1 laundering inflows in its lookback, R2 any laundering in the week, R3 laundering cross-border outflows in the week). Re-ran Day 2 and Day 3. Definition to be confirmed with AML experts.

finding: The agreed success criteria only limit R2 alerts, not total workload. Option E meets them, but total alerts stay almost the same because the longer R1 lookback doubles R1 alerts.
action: Add a criterion on total alerts or FTE before choosing an option. Present option D (fewer FTE, less detection) and option E (same workload, better alerts) as the decision.
